The Rime Lords taught that the self could be perfected. That the needs and frailties of the body could be purged. That the mind could free itself of the flesh and know the unseen world of spirits and fundamental forces. That the will could conquer all. The goal was nothing short of immortality, the preservation of the perfect self. For most of the Rime Lords’ mortal disciples, these teachings did little more than strengthen the body and clear the mind. But for some—the adepts—these teachings unlocked a fragment of their masters’ power. Rivalries were fierce among the adepts even when the Rime Lords walked the land. When the last Rime Lords disappeared, these rivalries flourished into schisms, sects, and violent purges. Some of the adepts fell. Others went into hiding. Still others passed their knowledge on, building schools and monasteries around them. To create an adept, start with the stats above. Pick or roll for an instinct and 1-4 moves to represent their capabilities.

They make their way north now and then: scoundrels, mercenaries, treasure-hunters… folk who just can’t make a go of a normal life. They’ll show up in Marshedge or Stonetop or Gordin’s Delve, in search of some big score. Or running from the consequences of the last one. Or both.

The Hillfolk (page 228) speak of dark times, when the Things Below (page 412) gave a gift to a petty chief. Depending on who tells the tale, it was a patch of loose soil or a deep pool of water, the hollow of a dool tree or a great cauldron of rusted iron. Regardless: a corpse placed within this vessel would rise as one of the Anan Gllo, the Empty Dead. The chief raised an undead army, and set out to make themselves king. Something interesting: The chief’s power was broken when a hero entered the vessel while still alive, giving their life to destroy it. A number of Anan Gllo linger, though, inert and waiting. Something useful: An Anan Gllo regains all its HP when it either drinks fresh blood or re-enters the vessel; it cannot otherwise regain HP. And every dawn, an Anan Gllo loses 1 HP. At 0 HP, it becomes inert until its HP are restored.

There are places where the wind dances constantly, fluttering and flitting, and here the andalau dwell. They are more prone to mischief than violence. Win their favor, and you might convince them to help you—especially if it involves going somewhere new or playing pranks. Just don’t be surprised when their attention flits elsewhere.

Among the southern well-to-do, the glorious past is a point of pride. Wealthy households keep pet scholars on retainer, and sponsor the study of ruins and antiquities. There’s a brisk trade in artifacts and relics. Collectors pay handsomely for items of true power. The south is full of ruins, but it’s also teeming with people. The best sites have already been dug up. But up north, at the World’s End? Why, one can barely swing a shovel without hitting some relic of the past, just waiting to be excavated. And studied. And sold.

Only in "civilized" lands is there such demand for murder that it’s an actual profession.

She appears out of the shadows, when the fear rises up to take you. Tall and grim and looming, draped in willow branches, moths flitting all about. She reaches out a bony hand. "Hush dear," she whispers. "Hush. Auntie Sallow is here to help." She was beautiful, once. The minder of a sacred grove. A place of clean water, butterflies, and bees. But then came war. Fire and poison and the sundering of earth. Schemes and lies. Grief and endless pain. ’Twas in grief that L’bin’bozia (page 421) found her. Gave her the strength to help. To find the innocent who suffered, the beautiful in despair. To offer succor, and the safety of her master’s cool embrace.

Big, powerful, wild cattle with horns longer than your arm and thicker than your hand can grip around. Even the does have big horns, and aren’t shy about using them.

instinct/selected/to-spook-or-to-get-ang.source: to spook or to get angry, in equal measure

The magic of the Roads and the open terrain make a life of banditry far from easy, but somehow, they crop up every few years. Might be Hillfolk, disgraced or desperate, but more often than not, they’re scoundrels who’d rather bleed their fellows than scrape by up in Gordin’s Delve.

Most bandit gangs struggle to find victims or shelter or both, and quickly die out or disband. The clever ones last a few seasons, but eventually folk catch wise and grow wary, and the bandits’ schemes start to fail. But every generation or so, a leader crops up who’s cagey enough to turn a gang of bandits into a serious threat. What does the chief possess that makes them such a threat? (pick 2 or 3) Agents in Gordin’s Delve and/or Marshedge A way to overcome the wards on the Roads Magic that can compel/lure/scare travelers off the Roads Magic that hides their crew, or changes their appearance Well-trained horses, or some other form of mobility A fortified hideout

As you might expect, grave robbing was always a problem for the Barrow Builders. But a clever sorcerer had a solution! So many hateful spirits roamed the world in those days. Why not bind some to the corpses of the deceased, and let the dead guard their own treasure?

Great big armored mustelids, like a cross between a stoat, a badger, and a pangolin, but like 6 feet long not counting the tail. They roam the Flats digging up burrows of just about anything, but they especially love to stir up a hlomren (page 134) nest and chomp chomp chomp. They’re far from the top of the food chain, though. If startled, they’ll spray musk and attempt to flee. If cornered, they’ll curl up and hope the attacker grows bored. A skilled tanner can turn a pair of hides into a magnificent ◇◇ beznpol scale coat (2 armor, warm, protects against acid, Value 3). Hillfolk champions are known to wear them.

These hulking brutes dwell in dark places: caves, north-facing slopes, and deep mountain forests. They’re hairy things, hunched and wild, only vaguely looking like people. They’d be little more than dangerous beasts, easily avoided, if they weren’t driven by an obsessive vice—and if they didn’t wield the wild elements themselves.

Like big crows with white-and-azure plumage. Their songs are piping and musical, playful and complex, sprinkled with actual voices and other unlikely sounds. A few dozen of them nest in the tower and the surrounding ruins. Smaller mischiefs nest in the Flats. Stormcatcher kept blue magpies as pets, and their descendants have passed down much oral lore. Sneak up on them, and you might overhear magpies telling each other tales that southern scholars would kill to know. Magpies find humans boorish, but fun to mess with, and they have such neat stuff. They love shiny objects, especially glass and fragments of larger things, and spend years making elaborate mosaics or piecing puzzles together.

They were the shining jewel in some Green Lord’s paradise, the bright beauty of a rising sun made flesh. They were happy and in love. (Or so they thought, for can a being bred to love truly do so?) Then their master’s tomb was plundered by the rebels. Their world was upended. They were bereft, vulnerable, alone and unloved. They had no interest in freedom, only the safe warm surety of other beings’ full regard. Fortunately, for them, such adoration was easy to find. Their domain is a stately pavilion in a summer glade, forever in that moment just before the dawn. It’s filled with fawning victims of their charms: lovers and would-be lovers, abducted children, devotees. And on the outskirts: the cast-out wretches, those who’ve lost favor but whose jealous adoration still feeds the Blush-of-Dawn.

Mostly they just lumber about the Steplands, looking for their favorite trees to tear up and chew through, sometimes clearing whole slopes. Just about everything gives them a wide berth, when they can. Even apex predators like a kleztigr don’t think they’re worth the trouble. You’d think that they’d be easy to spot and avoid, and mostly you’d be right. But sometimes you’ll round a bend or clear a slope and there one’ll be, just plodding along or munching on a log or taking a nap, and you’d best try to circle around, quiet-like.

It stands nearly 60 feet tall, a muscular Forge Lord cast in bronze. Similar statues loom about, each one grand and imposing. This statue, though, is shot through with blueish veins. And it feels like it’s watching you. Because it is. The colossus guards the entrance to its master’s domain. If someone approaches honorably, speaking in the Forge Lord’s tongue, it politely tells them to come again later, for its master is away. Intruders, blowhards, and thieves are dealt with forcibly. Something interesting: Those blueish veins are aetherium (page 404), and likely what animates the statue. Which, alas, means there’s no single weak-point. Maybe you could harm this thing by drawing the lightning from it. Something useful: Or you could, you know, just blast it with lightning and overload it.

About the size of a woodpecker, with black and wine-red plumage, flitting about in small flocks (2d6+4). Their laugh will make your blood run cold. But don’t worry. They’ll get your blood flowing again, real soon. Something interesting: Butcherbirds can smell fresh blood from miles away, and might descend on a hunter’s kill to gorge. Something useful: They can smell the blood of their own, and shun it; smeared butcherbird blood is an excellent repellent.

Are they crabs? Spiders? Hard to say. Whatever they are, they’ve got too many too-long limbs, shells that blend in with the rocky terrain, and an appetite for magical artifacts. They’ll drag their prizes back to their nests to feed. They can suck the power right out of minor trinkets, but powerful arcana can feed a small colony indefinitely. And yet, they keep venturing out to find more.

Bandits, beasts, and Hillfolk (page 234) are all a threat, and plenty of potential clients would just as soon steal a merchant’s goods as trade fairly for them. So, merchants hire guards. Great big silver-brown things, eating anything they can dig up or catch. They mostly hibernate through winter, and get especially bold and ornery in autumn as they try to fatten up. They’ve been known to wake up and forage even in winter, though. They lair in big caves, usually two mates and maybe their cubs. Out and about, the bulls are usually found on their own; the sows on their own, or with their cubs. They’re not usually aggressive towards people—unless surprised, extra hungry, or protecting the cubs. Then? Watch out.

A herd of wild horses has a life, nay, a spirit all its own, a spirit as free and fickle as the wind. Take care, you who would poach wild horses for your own purpose, lest you find your heart turned against you! Something interesting: "Ceffylwraig" means "horse wife," but she sees herself more as queen than wife: proud and haughty, disdainful of the weak and the slow, the herd her subjects more than her children. Something useful: A ceffylwraig is scornful and suspicious of praise or fancy words, but can be appeased by thoughtful gifts, offered with appropriate respect from proud women of noble bearing. What sort of gift do the ceffylwraig most value? What sort of gift will do in a pinch?

Majestic. Proud. Antlers so large you can scarce believe how deftly it moves through the woods. They are the royalty of deer. It is said that only the Pale Hunter can give them chase, and that any mortal who dares to stalk them quickly finds the tables turned.

The chosen shields are a chief’s best: the most loyal, the bravest, the bloodiest. They’re professional fighters, their chief’s bodyguards, enforcers, and lieutenants. They sit closest to the chief by the fire, and share the best haunches of meat. They take a share, too, of their chief’s loot and their chief’s glory. The wise chief lets them have it, for a chief is nothing without their chosen shields. And when a chief is toppled, it’s usually one of their chosen shields that does the toppling.

There is a burnt and blasted place, where the Steplands (page 372) abut Ferrier’s Fen (page 116). It once boasted a Stone Lord (page 382) fortress: grand, a tower eternal, lit by a fiery gem. But the servants rebelled. The seals were sundered. Ta’l Themyin, the Burning Child, shattered the gem and toppled the tower and laughed and laughed and laughed. His rage still boils to the surface, poisoning any beast bold enough to forage in these ruins. His cruelty sends them forth, to uproot and topple, to sunder and burn.

The Forge Lords burned with an inner fire, a fire that threatened to consume them even when they lived. And when they died badly—slowly, desperately, betrayed and full of helpless rage—that fire could linger on. First it would burn away the Forge Lord’s flesh, and then its spirit, and then its soul. And then it would wait in the bones, like heat in banked coals. Wait for fresh air to give it new life, and fresh souls to burn for fuel.

They’re not really shaped like spiders, but that’s what they make you think of. Picture a metal basket, holding gears and springs and a glowing central core. Articulated legs extend out, each ending in a little 3-clawed pincer. They squeak as they move, their many joints needing oil. They were made to be little servants, extra sets of hands to help around a house or forge. Even now, they’re just trying to help.

Each thorn on a plant is a sword, brandished boldly against a world that would defile its flowers, steal its fruit, and devour its delicate buds. What, then, are the coedwaig? Only Danu’s swords, brandished by the Mother herself in defense of her most beautiful and vulnerable children.

They don’t usually hunt people. But when game is scarce, or some fool provokes them, they sometimes get a taste for human blood. Even then, they mostly leave groups alone, waiting for someone to fall behind or wander off. Mostly.

Especially if the person leading them is someone they trust, or respect, or admire. And if that first little dark deed comes without any consequences, or any consequences to them? The vaunted "tree adder," most lethal serpent in the Wood, up to 6 feet long and dripping with venom. In warm months, they hunt and bask in the canopy or sunny clearings. In colder months, they hide in hollows and under logs, going into torpor in winter. They don’t hunt people, but they don’t fear them either. When you are bitten by a cwisarff, mark a debility in addition to taking damage. Until the poison is treated, you can’t regain

A frill of feathered quills sprouts from its neck and runs down its back. Maybe a half-dozen of them stalk the whole Great Wood, and one hasn’t been spotted near Stonetop for generations (Tor be praised). Something interesting: They prey mostly on large game (wisents, tal gerdwyr, etc.). They’ll attack people, but rarely hunt them. Something useful: They attack people to establish dominance, seeing us as rivals. An appropriate offering or show of obeisance might calm one enough for you to get the hell out of there.

She turned up in Gordin’s Delve years back, and one of the Bosses put her to work as an enforcer. They keep her sauced and happy, until there’s work to be done. Then they dry her out, point out the target, and stand back.

Or sent back by their fellow victims. Or guided back by one of the Lady’s own crows. They dig themselves free of their graves, reborn and whole. And vengeance shall be theirs.

Dool spirits hail from beyond the Last Door. They are not undead, for they never lived, but are native to the afterlife. They sometimes slip into this world, haunting the dool trees (page 73) from which they get their name. When a dool spirit takes a liking to a victim’s fears, it leaves its tree and binds itself to that victim’s very bones. It proceeds to haunt them, and only them, driving them mad with fear. Imagine one of those artists’ mannequins, but full-sized and made of polished rock. Two fingers and a thumb on each hand. Faceless, expressionless, making a stone-on-stone grinding noise as they move. They’re most often found inert and covered in dust, waiting for some energy source— like a Stone Lord’s song or a thrumming power-crystal—to give them "life." They’ll then follow any orders given to them in the Stone Lord’s tongue. A few of these servants are still active, powered by inexhaustible sources in ancient halls. Their joints are worn smooth, their feet and hands ground down to nubs. Some crawl on broken limbs, attempting to complete tasks that will never end.

Everyone knows to shun deep, still water, and the llamudwr (or "water leapers") are surely one reason why. Take the body of a frog, 6 or 7 feet long. Add another 8 or 9 feet of whipping tail, tipped with a venomous barb. Get rid of its legs, not even stumps, but give it bat wings, a span of nearly 20 feet unfurled. Hide it in a lake or fen, away from the sun’s cruel light. And finally, make it hungry. Very, very hungry.

Each one is a few feet long, like a cuttlefish crossed with a giant maggot, squirming wet and gray, a face full of feelers whose touch stings like lightning. They spend most of their lives in the water, congregating near power-crystals (page 389) and aetherium artifacts (page 404) that have been claimed by the river. They seem entranced by the passive energy, almost lulled to sleep. But when they sense something more dynamic, something meatier, they wriggle out of the water fast enough. Some Hillfolk claim that luglfsk are just tadpoles, and tell stories of larger, many-legged terrors that fling lightning from face-feelers that stretch as long as a man grows tall. But those are probably just spook-stories to scare travelers. Probably.

Creatures of the first age, things of fire and stone. They’re segmented, 3’ thick and 20’ long, covered in overlapping plates that glow red at the seams. The air heat-shimmers around them. They have no eyes, just a great mouth-opening and concentric rows of grinding teeth that melt and burrow through rock. Winding tunnels stretch behind them, lined with slag hardened into ropy stone. The worms described here are mere centuries old, the ones most likely to be encountered. Older and larger ones survive in the Deeps, up to 10’ wide and over a 100’ long (huge, +6 HP, +2 damage and roll 1d12 instead of 1d10). In eons past, even larger worms carved out much of the Labyrinth.

Every able-bodied youth does their turn at their chief’s hillfort. They spend a year or two drilling, marching, learning the spear, and standing in the shield wall. They sing songs, and talk big, and maybe even get their hands red. A few are picked for their chief’s standing force, but most head home to their hamlets, prepared to defend their families and swell their chief ’s ranks when called. That’s the idea, at least.

No longer young, no longer eager or scared. Just grim folk with something to fight for, something to lose. They might not be as spry as once they were, but they’re no strangers to the black business.

The Rime Lords created these mighty spirits to act as emissaries and spies. A few still remain, tethered to the meditation-halls in which they were made but roaming the Whitefangs in search of novelty and diversion. They have grown bored in their masters’ absence, and from boredom has grown a subtle cruelty. The people of the Whitefangs treat them with respect, for they are still the emissaries of the Rime Lords. But they also know better than to trust their counsel.

The spirits of even shallow ponds can be callous and uncaring. How much worse, then, are the spirits of those deeper pools that have claimed the lives of mortals? For—willing or not—they have made offering to Daagon, and let it in to their watery hearts. When you listen to the morgais’ song or let your gaze linger on its graceful form, your heart fills with longing. If you go to it willingly, mark XP. If you wish to turn away, roll +WIS: on a 10+, you see the ugliness beneath and can think clearly; on a 7-9, you shake yourself free but the longing remains—mark miserable or dazed (your choice); on a 6-, you approach before you realize what you’re doing.

Stone Lords adorned their halls with elaborate tilework and mosaics. Most of them were decorative. Most of them. Something interesting: Either some spirit is possessing these tiles, or this is some sort of construct. If it’s a spirit, there must be a tether. If it’s a Stone Lord construct, well, the individual tiles are too small to power or direct themselves. Something useful: The mosaic’s frame remained on the wall, and it’s glowing blue—aetherium runes! Destroy the runes, and the construct should fall apart.

Like orangutans but taller, more powerfully built, with thick, shaggy white hair. They dwell in small bands, in Rime Lord ruins (page 320) or sacred sites (page 362) that are far from any well-trod trails. They venture out to hunt and gather, but avoid people as much as they can. Each band of mountain apes collects things: a particular type of plant or flower, the bones of certain animals, bits of writing, dark ice (page 322), etc. They keep these hoards in a central place, hidden away, revered and treasured even more than their own children or their lives. Particularly large or well-established bands will have an alpha (large, leader, +6 HP, +1 damage) who does nothing but protect the hoard.

They lie entombed, their corpses embalmed, their souls bound to the heavily-warded canopic jars that store their most-vital organs. Yet those souls linger forever in Fae-woven realms of glamour and delight. In these realms, the Green Lords are as gods. They are loathe to leave them, and rarely need to. But should their existence be truly threatened, they will return to this world of base flesh, inhabit their long-dead bodies, and punish any intruders with the savagery of the cruelest beasts.

When the Fae rebelled, some of the Green Lord’s mortal servants—the ancestors of the Forest Folk (page 150)—sided with the traitors. But not all. Most remained loyal, or at least too afraid of their masters to risk turning on them. Their loyalty, alas, did not save them. At first, the Green Lords would plant demon-seeds in only the bodies of servants who had already fallen. But when they saw just how effective those animated corpses were, well… the Green Lords were nothing if not practical. Many of these horrors remain in Vor Svetelik, bound by orders to protect the city or certain sites within. Thank the gods they were not allowed to roam free.

The Nerth Tree grows in the Great Wood. It can only be found by one mortal each midsummer, by following a particular path in the woods (page 516). The roots are littered with bones of former supplicants. Hanging from the tree: a great serpent. Crush it and eats its heart, and you will gain its vitality. But good luck with that.

Many tales tell of a stranger met in an unlikely place. The stranger is in some sort of pickle, or challenges our hero, or presents a tempting opportunity. Whatever else happens, the stranger ends up vanishing, but not before our hero notices his missing finger—and realizes that they just met Tor. When the tale’s hero rises to the occasion, they win a gift from the stranger: a treasure or a magic item, a secret or a prophecy, or maybe just some useful bit of advice. But when the "hero" comes up short, they wind up cursed or "win" some treasure that brings them ruin and woe.

The Stone Lords would deploy them among the rowdier servants to keep things running smoothly. When you are in range of a pacifier’s hum, your emotions lose their edge. When you rouse yourself to act violently, urgently, or passionately, roll +WIS. If you are in range of multiple pacifiers humming in unison, you have disadvantage. On a 10+, you shake off the effect; on a 7-9, you shake off the effect but pick 1. Your mind is addled; mark dazed Your freedom is short-lived; the effect returns if you pause for any reason You get carried away or take things too far, resulting in a consequence of the GM’s choice

Ferocedes once had dozens of constructs to defend and maintain the tower. But the years have not been kind. Only ten or so remain, and one or two are usually offline for modifications or repairs. Each one has an ◇ aetherium core (magical, fragile, Value 2 to the right buyer). Ferocedes can repair minor damage to a core, and/or install it in a new body, but he can’t make new ones without the aetherium crucible (page 405). Each construct is generally humanoid, though most lack a "head" and all are made of mismatched parts. Pick or roll a current task for each. What becomes of a dead tree’s spirit? Most linger as simple log-spirits, weakening as the log rots to mulch. But when generations of trees grow and die in the same place, they might become something more. Something that defends the grove, and its current trees, and all the trees that are yet to come.

When an untethered ghost (page 76) or a shade (page 85) possesses an empty corpse, it becomes a pyped. They are wretched things, all rotting flesh and lurching movements, hungering for sweet marrow, scavenging on carrion and graves. But hunger can make them bold. Bold enough to hunt the weak and sick at the edge of a village, or a lone traveler caught unawares. Pypeds rise only from corpses that are relatively intact, and which have not undergone proper funeral rites. If a pyped is destroyed, the spirit within will seek a new, viable corpse. A shade must find one before the sun banishes it. An untethered ghost must find one before its memories fade and it becomes a wraith (page 79).

When a boar lives long enough, and survives enough close calls, and dines year after year on the roots and nuts of ferro trees, it eventually becomes a raselbaedd. The size of a horse, with tusks like short spears and a hide that’s crisscrossed with scars and that bristles with broken blades. When you deal 2 damage or less to a raselbaedd, before armor, your weapon chips or shatters on its hide. A raselbaedd’s hide (immobile, Value 2) can be harvested by a competent hunter with a fine steel blade (2 piercing, Value 2). It can then be fashioned into 1d4 ◇ raselbaedd cuirasses (2 armor, Value 3). Doing so requires: An exceptional tanner An upgraded workshop with fine steel tools (Value 3) A season of labor per cuirass

Hunched humanoid forms carved of wood, with great wings, taloned feet, and heads crowned with branch-like antlers. They were made by the Green Lords to be sentinels and guardians, to watch over their borders and their most important sites. Now, ages and generations later, they still watch, and wait, and protect their nests. Something interesting: The tales say that the song of a redbreasted bluebird will keep the rhagedn still, letting folk pass unmolested. Something useful: It just so happens that you know how to whistle the tune (whether or not you can whistle it well enough is questionable).

Only thirteen Rime Lords survive; each remains in stasis in some key place of power. Their spirits are merged in an eternal dance and song, continuously weaving the dark ice glacier that keeps the voice of Y’aaw’kara bound and prevents madness from spreading unchecked across the world. Pray, o mortal. Pray that they continue their vigil. Pray that their wills do not falter. Pray that no interloper is so foolish as to disturb them. Pray for your family, your friends, and all that you know. Pray that they do not wake.

But people in the water are clumsy and oblivious. So when a screech eel spots someone in the water, it calls out to its friends. And when enough of them have gathered, they feast.

A shade can ride a living, willing host, or one who has been properly prepared (with arcane markings, by bearing an appropriate object, via a potion, etc.). It can withstand daylight while doing so, but only with great effort. It experiences what its host experiences, and can communicate with its host via only impulse and desire. And they hope that their sacrifices—given in bulk in late autumn—will keep their dark gods satiated while the suarachan sleep through winter. They have exacting tastes, far more subtle and refined than any of their peers. But should you embarrass, defy, or simply bore one, expect to be brutally devoured. Few of these creatures survive, thankfully. The Fae hunt them and they shun others of their kind, jealous of territory and wealth. But every dozen years or so, some urge drives them all to the ruins of Vor Svetelik (page 468), entourage in tow, where they engage in ostentatious displays and mating rituals. There, amidst the sick white trees, the next brood of swyn are seeded. There, perhaps, these foul things might be wiped out once and for all. Sometimes, out on the Flats, you’ll see what looks to be small hills in the distance. I advise you to steer clear. They probably aren’t hills, really, but huge piles of dirt that a thunder drake has moved as it digs. And hoo boy, you do not want to stumble into one of them on their home turf. Something interesting: Thunder drakes eat mostly grass and shrubs, but they have a taste for certain ores. They spend their time grazing, sleeping, and digging up rocks. Something useful: They particularly savor the taste of copper, and relish aetherium (page 404). If they find a source of it, they’ll chew it right up and spend the next few days belching lightning bolts. When you are near a thunder drake when it bellows, roll +CON: on a 10+, pick 1; on a 7-9, pick 2; on a 6-, all 3. These grey-white rattlesnakes grow to absurd size, big enough to eat a boar, a deer, or even a person. Manmarchers say that they haunt the bluffs and ruins along the river, waiting months, years, or even decades between meals. While most rattlesnakes rattle to warn off threats or predators, totnatter use their rattles to hunt. They delight in the terror their rattle causes, and use it even when they could just bite their prey unawares. When a totnatter pumps its prey full of venom, start the following countdown: l Their hands shake, their bodies shiver (mark weakened) l They grow confused, thinking things that aren’t true (mark dazed) l They struggle to breathe, to keep going (mark miserable) l They are dying (roll for Death’s Door)

Then the blizzard rolled in. And that’s how Ulliam died. But say what you will about Ulliam, he loved his wife and kids. Still does. Dragged his frozen self home to see ’em again. He knows they can’t see him like this, but he can’t keep himself from lurking. And when some lech comes sniffing around his wife, or some fool notices him and makes a fuss… well, there’s only so much a man can take. And that little spark of warmth he draws out of them? At the base of the gorge is a thin split in reality, a vortex, a manifestation of Hlad the Devourer, sucking in everything it touches. The mountain and the gorge are shunned now. The Hillfolk (page 228) and the Ustrina (page 464) who live nearby know better than to approach. But the Barrow Builders (page 34) fed the vortex. They brought it gifts, and offerings, and living, screaming sacrifice. In time, these offerings gave the vortex a Voice. And the Voice roams the mountain still.

Wraiths are cursed with endless hunger. They are damaged souls, wounded by dark magic, another wraith, or the dehumanizing effects of starvation or addiction. They are little more than beasts, driven by the emptiness within, with only the vaguest sense of who they once were. Other ghosts might become wraiths when their tethers are destroyed. If they linger in the world, they find themselves filled with gnawing need, and must sustain themselves on the living. These unbound wraiths are weaker, but often form packs with others of their kind (group, vicious instead of stealthy, 13 HP each, d8 damage, afraid of firelight). When a wraith reduces you to 0 HP and you survive, your soul is wounded. Reduce your max HP by 4. Until your soul is healed, your instinct becomes "Hunger: to fill the emptiness inside you with excess," and should you roll a 6- on Death’s Door, you die and become a wraith (a monster in the GM’s control).
